chunks: "A camera is basically a lens that projects the scene onto a chip full of tiny light meters. The lens focuses light so every point in the scene lands on one spot on the sensor.
Each pixel is a photodiode: photons hit silicon, knock electrons loose by the photoelectric effect, and the pixel collects those electrons during the exposure time.
More light or a longer exposure means more electrons.
On top of each pixel there's a microlens to funnel light in, and a red, green or blue color filter in the Bayer pattern, because a photodiode only counts photons and can't tell colors apart.
When the exposure ends, the charge in each pixel is converted to a voltage, amplified by an analog gain, which is what ISO really is, and digitized by an ADC, usually 10 to 12 bits on a phone.

Then the image signal processor does the rest: it fixes bad pixels and lens shading, demosaics to get full color at every pixel, applies white balance and a color matrix, denoises, tone-maps, sharpens, and compresses to JPEG or HEIC.
The autofocus, auto exposure and white-balance loop runs in the background to set the lens position, exposure time and gain for the next frame.
So the chain is optics, sensor, ADC, ISP, with a control loop wrapped around it."
